attrs.why: The radiologist's new finding of a lower gastrointestinal contrast study showing no passage of rectal contrast beyond the anal canal directly reinforces the anal/rectal obstruction already suggested by the catheter that could not be advanced more than half an inch. Combined with absent meconium, bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, multiple dilated bowel loops with an S-shaped sigmoid extending toward the pelvis, term birth, and a normally positioned anus, anorectal malformation is strongly supported. Confidence is raised from 0.85 to 0.88.

The new lower gastrointestinal contrast study showing no rectal contrast passage argues further against Hirschsprung disease, which would typically demonstrate a transition zone with proximal dilation and a narrowed distal segment rather than complete blockage. Together with the catheter obstruction at the anal opening, this reduces the likelihood of Hirschsprung disease from 0.3 to 0.2.

The new lower gastrointestinal contrast finding of no passage of rectal contrast is inconsistent with meconium ileus/atresia, in which contrast would typically outline a microcolon and dilated proximal bowel rather than being blocked at the anorectal level. Combined with the catheter obstruction located at the anus rather than at an ileal level, confidence decreases from 0.15 to 0.12.
node-5 normal echo, renal ultrasound, vertebral X-ray refute VACTERL

attrs.why: The catheter could be inserted half an inch before becoming blocked, suggesting some proximal anal canal patency rather than a completely blind imperforate anus, while the new lower GI contrast study confirms a distal anorectal-level obstruction and the anus sits in a normal position with well-developed gluteal folds. These features favor a low-type anorectal malformation with a partially patent anal canal. Confidence is moderate (0.5) because the exact anatomical subtype has not been directly demonstrated.
